1 The hidden this pointer

1.1 From self to this

In Python, every method’s first parameter, by convention called self, refers to the object the method was called on:

class Fraction:
    def __init__(self, numerator, denominator):
        self.numerator = numerator
        self.denominator = denominator

In Chapter 11 we met C++’s version, this. Now let’s look at it properly: it plays the role of self, but it’s a pointer, and you never write it as a parameter.

1.2 The hidden this pointer

hidden_pointer_this.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Simple {
  private:
    double value{};

  public:
    Simple(double value) : value{value} {}

    double get_value() const { return value; } // same as this->value
    void set_value(double value) { this->value = value; }
    void print() const { std::cout << this->value << '\n'; }
};

int main() {
    Simple simple{0.0};
    std::cout << simple.get_value() << '\n';
    simple.set_value(42.5);
    simple.print();
    return 0;
}
0
42.5

Inside every member function, this holds the address of the implicit object. Select its members with -> (Chapter 11).

1.3 How is this set?

When we write simple.set_value(42.5);, the compiler (conceptually) turns it into an ordinary function call, with the object’s address as an extra, hidden argument:

Simple::set_value(&simple, 42.5); // not real C++: just what happens underneath

So in each call, this points at whichever object the function was called on:

Simple a{1.0}; // inside the constructor: this == &a
Simple b{2.0}; // inside the constructor: this == &b
a.set_value(12); // inside set_value():  this == &a
b.set_value(21); // inside set_value():  this == &b

In a const member function, this points to a const object: that’s where Chapter 10’s error message “passing ‘const Date’ as ‘this’ argument” came from.

1.4 When to write this explicitly

Most of the time we don’t: a plain value already means this->value. We need it when a parameter has the same name as a member:

struct Something {
    double data{};

    void set_data(double data) {
        this->data = data; // this->data is the member; data is the parameter
    }
};

1.5 Returning *this: method chaining

You’ve been chaining calls since Chapter 01:

std::cout << "Hello, " << user_name;
// is evaluated as
(std::cout << "Hello, ") << user_name;

(std::cout << "Hello, ") prints, and then returns std::cout itself, ready for the next <<. Our member functions can do the same: return *this, the implicit object, by reference.

This is called method chaining (or function chaining). We’ll come back to it in Chapter 13, when we write our own <<.

1.6 Method chaining in action

method_chaining_example.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Calculator {
  private:
    double value{};

  public:
    Calculator(double value) : value{value} {}

    Calculator& add(double x) {
        value += x;
        return *this; // return the implicit object itself
    }
    Calculator& mult(double x) {
        value *= x;
        return *this;
    }
    double get_value() const { return value; }
};

int main() {
    Calculator calc{42};
    calc.add(5).add(-3).mult(4); // method chaining
    std::cout << calc.get_value() << '\n';
    return 0;
}
176

Each function returns a reference to the same object. Return by value instead, and each call would work on a copy!

1.7 Method chaining, in a picture

calc.add(5) changes calc and returns calc itself, so .add(-3) is called on calc too, and so on. That’s exactly how std::cout << a << b works.

2 Destructors

2.1 The cleanup problem

Remember memory leaks from Chapter 09? Here’s a class that allocates memory when it’s created:

database_helper_without_destructor.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

class DatabaseHelper {
  private:
    std::string* connection{}; // allocated on the heap

  public:
    DatabaseHelper(const std::string& path)
        : connection{new std::string{path}} {
        std::cout << "Connected to " << *connection << '\n';
    }
};

int main() {
    {
        DatabaseHelper db{"127.0.0.1:5432/my_database"};
    } // db is destroyed here... but nobody deletes *connection
    return 0;
}

2.2 AddressSanitizer agrees

$ g++ -std=c++20 -g -fsanitize=address database_helper_without_destructor.cpp
$ ./a.out
Connected to 127.0.0.1:5432/my_database
==3376==ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks
Direct leak of 32 byte(s) in 1 object(s) allocated from:
    #1 in DatabaseHelper::DatabaseHelper(const std::string&) ...cpp:10
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 59 byte(s) leaked in 2 allocation(s).

(Output shortened.) db is destroyed at the end of its block, but the std::string it created with new on line 10 is never deleted. And connection is private, so main() can’t delete it either.

2.3 A cleanup() function?

database_helper_with_cleanup.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

class DatabaseHelper {
  private:
    std::string* connection{};

  public:
    DatabaseHelper(const std::string& path)
        : connection{new std::string{path}} {
        std::cout << "Connected to " << *connection << '\n';
    }

    void cleanup() { // the user must remember to call this
        delete connection;
        connection = nullptr;
        std::cout << "Cleaned up\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    {
        DatabaseHelper db{"127.0.0.1:5432/my_database"};
        db.cleanup(); // forget this line, and memory leaks
    }
    return 0;
}
Connected to 127.0.0.1:5432/my_database
Cleaned up

It works, but every user must remember to call cleanup(). Someone, someday, will forget.

2.4 Destructors to the rescue

A destructor is a special member function that runs automatically when an object is destroyed, so the class can clean up after itself.

  • Its name is the class name with a tilde in front: ~Simple().
  • It takes no arguments and has no return type.
  • A class has exactly one destructor.

Constructors set an object up; destructors tidy it away.

2.5 A first destructor

destructor_example.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Simple {
  private:
    int id{};

  public:
    Simple(int id) : id{id} { std::cout << "Constructing " << id << '\n'; }
    ~Simple() { std::cout << "Destructing " << id << '\n'; } // destructor
};

int main() {
    Simple simple1{1};
    {
        Simple simple2{2};
    } // simple2 is destroyed here
    Simple simple3{3};
    return 0;
} // simple3, then simple1, are destroyed here
Constructing 1
Constructing 2
Destructing 2
Constructing 3
Destructing 3
Destructing 1

2.6 When do destructors run?

  • A local object is destroyed at the end of the block where it was created, just like local variables in Chapter 02.
  • Objects in the same block are destroyed in reverse order of creation: last constructed, first destroyed.
  • If you don’t write a destructor, the compiler writes an empty implicit destructor. If there’s nothing to clean up, that’s all you need.

2.7 The database helper, fixed

database_helper.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

class DatabaseHelper {
  private:
    std::string* connection{};

  public:
    DatabaseHelper(const std::string& path)
        : connection{new std::string{path}} {
        std::cout << "Connected to " << *connection << '\n';
    }

    ~DatabaseHelper() { // called automatically: nothing to remember
        std::cout << "Disconnecting from " << *connection << '\n';
        delete connection;
    }
};

int main() {
    {
        DatabaseHelper db{"127.0.0.1:5432/my_database"};
    } // the destructor runs right here
    std::cout << "db is gone, and so is its memory\n";
    return 0;
}
Connected to 127.0.0.1:5432/my_database
Disconnecting from 127.0.0.1:5432/my_database
db is gone, and so is its memory

Nothing to remember, and AddressSanitizer reports no leaks.

2.8 RAII: let objects clean up after themselves

The pattern we just used has a name: RAII, Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (a famously bad name for a great idea).

  • Acquire a resource (memory, a file, a network connection) in the constructor.
  • Release it in the destructor.

Then the resource lives exactly as long as the object, and cleanup can never be forgotten.

ImportantKey idea

This is how std::string, std::vector and std::unique_ptr (Chapter 09) manage their memory. Now you know how it’s done!

2.9 A class template that owns an array

array_with_destructor.cpp
#include <iostream>

template <typename T, int N> // a type AND a value (Chapter 06)
class FixedArray {
    T* data{}; // private by default

  public:
    FixedArray(const T& value) : data{new T[N]} { // acquire...
        for (int i{0}; i < N; ++i) {              // i < N, not i <= N!
            data[i] = value;
        }
    }
    ~FixedArray() {    // ...and release
        delete[] data; // new[] needs delete[] (Chapter 09)
        std::cout << "Memory returned\n";
    }
    T get(int i) const { return data[i]; }
};

int main() {
    FixedArray<double, 5> numbers{4.2};
    std::cout << numbers.get(0) << ' ' << numbers.get(4) << '\n';
    return 0;
} // no cleanup() call needed
4.2 4.2
Memory returned

FixedArray is a class template with a type parameter T and a value parameter N (more on class templates shortly).

Note delete[], and i < N: writing data[N] would be out of bounds.

2.10 Watch out: copying an object that owns memory

shallow_copy_problem.cpp
#include <iostream>

class IntBox { // owns one int on the heap
  private:
    int* data{};

  public:
    IntBox(int value) : data{new int{value}} {}
    ~IntBox() { delete data; }

    int get() const { return *data; }
};

int main() {
    IntBox a{42};
    IntBox b{a}; // copies the POINTER, not the int
    std::cout << a.get() << ' ' << b.get() << '\n';
    return 0;
} // b's destructor deletes the int... then a's deletes it again!
$ ./shallow_copy_problem
42 42
free(): double free
detected in tcache 2
Aborted

It printed fine, then crashed on the way out. Why?

2.11 What went wrong: a shallow copy

The implicit copy constructor copies each member. The member is a pointer, so b gets the same address as a: a shallow copy. When main() ends, both destructors delete the same int. Undefined behaviour, and here a crash.

2.12 The rule of three (and of zero)

TipBest practice: the rule of three

If a class needs a destructor, it almost certainly also needs its own copy constructor and copy assignment (Chapter 13), or must forbid copying with = delete (Chapter 11).

Better still, follow the rule of zero: let members that already manage themselves (std::vector, std::string, std::unique_ptr) own the resources. Then you need no destructor, and the implicit copy does the right thing.

3 Class templates

3.1 The same problem, for classes

We met this problem for functions in Chapter 06:

struct PairInt {
    int first{};
    int second{};
};

struct PairDouble {
    double first{};
    double second{};
};

And a pair of std::vector<double>s? Of strings? You’ve already used the answer: std::vector<double> is a class template.

3.2 Class templates

A class template is a recipe for making class types, just as a function template is a recipe for functions.

pair_class_template.cpp
#include <iostream>

template <typename T> // the template parameter declaration
struct Pair {
    T first{};
    T second{};
};

int main() {
    Pair<int> p1{5, 6}; // instantiates Pair<int>
    std::cout << p1.first << ' ' << p1.second << '\n';

    Pair<double> p2{1.2, 3.4}; // instantiates Pair<double>
    std::cout << p2.first << ' ' << p2.second << '\n';

    Pair<double> p3{7.8, 9.0}; // reuses Pair<double>
    std::cout << p3.first << ' ' << p3.second << '\n';
    return 0;
}
5 6
1.2 3.4
7.8 9

Start with template <typename T>, then write the struct or class as usual, using T. Use it as Pair<int>, Pair<double>, …

3.3 What the compiler generates

pair_class_template_compiler_pov.cpp
#include <iostream>

template <typename T>
struct Pair; // only the declaration is left

template <> // what the compiler generates for T = int...
struct Pair<int> {
    int first{};
    int second{};
};

template <> // ...and for T = double
struct Pair<double> {
    double first{};
    double second{};
};

int main() {
    Pair<int> p1{5, 6};
    std::cout << p1.first << ' ' << p1.second << '\n';
    Pair<double> p2{1.2, 3.4};
    std::cout << p2.first << ' ' << p2.second << '\n';
    return 0;
}
5 6
1.2 3.4

As with function templates, the compiler stamps out one real class per type you use, Pair<int> and Pair<double>. You never write template <> like this yourself: it just shows you what happens.

3.4 Class templates and function templates together

class_template_and_func_template.cpp
#include <iostream>

template <typename T>
struct Pair {
    T first{};
    T second{};
};

template <typename T>
constexpr T max(Pair<T> p) { // a function template taking a Pair<T>
    return (p.first < p.second) ? p.second : p.first;
}

int main() {
    Pair<int> p1{5, 6};
    std::cout << max<int>(p1) << " is larger\n"; // T given explicitly

    Pair<double> p2{1.2, 3.4};
    std::cout << max(p2) << " is larger\n"; // T deduced (prefer this)
    return 0;
}
6 is larger
3.4 is larger

For the call max(p1), the compiler instantiates Pair<int> and the function int max<int>(Pair<int> p). constexpr (Chapter 06) lets the compiler run max() at compile time when the arguments are known then.

3.5 Several template types

class_multiple_template_types.cpp
#include <iostream>

template <typename T, typename U>
struct Pair {
    T first{};
    U second{};
};

template <typename T, typename U>
void print(const Pair<T, U>& p) {
    std::cout << '[' << p.first << ", " << p.second << "]\n";
}

int main() {
    Pair<int, double> p1{1, 2.3}; // an int and a double
    Pair<double, int> p2{4.5, 6}; // a double and an int
    Pair<int, int> p3{7, 8};      // two ints
    print(p1);
    print(p2);
    print(p3);
    return 0;
}
[1, 2.3]
[4.5, 6]
[7, 8]

3.6 std::pair: the standard library’s version

Pairs of values are so common that the standard library has exactly this class template, std::pair in <utility>, with members first and second:

std_pair_example.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <utility> // for std::pair

auto max(const auto& pair) { // abbreviated function template (Ch. 06)
    return (pair.first < pair.second) ? pair.second : pair.first;
}

int main() {
    std::pair<int, double> p1{1, 2.3};
    std::pair<double, int> p2{4.5, 6};
    std::cout << "max(p1) = " << max(p1) << '\n';
    std::cout << "max(p2) = " << max(p2) << '\n';
    std::cout << p1.first << ' ' << p1.second << '\n';
    return 0;
}
max(p1) = 2.3
max(p2) = 6
1 2.3

4 Friends

4.1 Why friends?

You’ve written std::cout << x; countless times. << is an operator with two operands, std::cout and x, much like a + b.

For our own classes, we’d love to write std::cout << polynomial;. The function behind that << needs to see the polynomial’s private data, but it can’t be a member of our class (Chapter 13 explains why).

C++’s answer: make it a friend.

4.2 Friendship

  • Inside a class, a friend declaration (friend ...;) names a function or class that gets full access to this class’s private (and protected) members.
  • That function or class is a friend.
ImportantKey idea

Friendship is always granted by the class whose members will be accessed. It can’t be claimed by the function or class that wants access.

4.3 A friend non-member function

friend_nonmember_function.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Accumulator {
  private:
    double value{};

  public:
    void add(double x) { value += x; }

    // print() is not a member, but it may use our private members
    friend void print(const Accumulator& accumulator);
};

void print(const Accumulator& accumulator) { // not a member!
    std::cout << accumulator.value << '\n';  // allowed: it's a friend
}

int main() {
    Accumulator acc{};
    acc.add(42);
    print(acc); // called like any non-member function
    return 0;
}
42

print() is an ordinary non-member function, but Accumulator declared it a friend, so it may read accumulator.value.

4.4 Defining a friend inside the class

friend_nonmember_function_inside_class.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Accumulator {
  private:
    double value{};

  public:
    void add(double x) { value += x; }

    // Defined inside the class, but still NOT a member function
    friend void print(const Accumulator& accumulator) {
        std::cout << accumulator.value << '\n';
    }
};

int main() {
    Accumulator acc{};
    acc.add(5);
    print(acc); // not acc.print()
    return 0;
}
5

Even though print() is defined inside Accumulator, it is not a member: we call it as print(acc), not acc.print().

4.5 A friend of several classes

function_friend_with_multiple_classes.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Humidity;     // forward declaration: used before it's defined
class Temperature { // members are private by default
    int temp{};

  public:
    Temperature(int temp) : temp{temp} {}
    friend void print_weather(const Temperature& t, const Humidity& h);
};

class Humidity {
    int humidity{};

  public:
    Humidity(int humidity) : humidity{humidity} {}
    friend void print_weather(const Temperature& t, const Humidity& h);
};

void print_weather(const Temperature& t, const Humidity& h) {
    std::cout << t.temp << " degrees, " << h.humidity << "% humidity\n";
}

int main() {
    print_weather(Temperature{12}, Humidity{10});
    return 0;
}
12 degrees, 10% humidity

class Humidity; is a forward declaration of a class, needed because Temperature mentions Humidity before it’s defined.

4.6 Prefer non-friend functions

prefer_nonfriend_to_friend_01.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Accumulator {
  private:
    int value{};

  public:
    void add(int x) { value += x; }
    friend void print(const Accumulator& acc);
};

void print(const Accumulator& acc) { std::cout << acc.value << '\n'; }

int main() {
    Accumulator acc{};
    acc.add(5);
    print(acc);
    return 0;
}
5

This works, but print() depends on a private detail. Rename value, and print() breaks too.

4.7 …when a public member will do

prefer_nonfriend_to_friend_02.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Accumulator {
  private:
    int value{};

  public:
    void add(int x) { value += x; }
    int get_value() const { return value; }
};

void print(const Accumulator& acc) { std::cout << acc.get_value() << '\n'; }

int main() {
    Accumulator acc{};
    acc.add(5);
    print(acc);
    return 0;
}
5

With a public getter, print() needs no friendship, and doesn’t care what the member is called.

TipBest practice

Prefer non-friend functions when the public interface is enough.

4.8 Friend classes

friend_class_example.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Storage {
  private:
    int int_value{};
    double double_value{};

  public:
    Storage(int i, double d) : int_value{i}, double_value{d} {}
    friend class Display; // Display may use our private members
};

class Display {
  public:
    void show(const Storage& s) const { // allowed: Display is a friend
        std::cout << s.int_value << ' ' << s.double_value << '\n';
    }
};

int main() {
    Storage storage{5, 6.7};
    Display display{};
    display.show(storage);
    return 0;
}
5 6.7

A friend class may use the private members of the class that befriends it: every member function of Display can read a Storage’s private data.

4.9 Friendship has limits

  1. It isn’t mutual. Display is a friend of Storage, but Storage is not a friend of Display, unless Display says so too.
  2. It isn’t transitive. If A is a friend of B, and B is a friend of C, A is still not a friend of C.
  3. It isn’t inherited. If A befriends B, classes derived from B (Chapter 14) are not friends of A.

4.10 Friend member functions (self-study)

Instead of befriending a whole class, you can befriend a single member function. It takes some care with the order of definitions, so this part is for self-study. We’ll build it up in three attempts.

4.11 Attempt 1: the friend’s class isn’t defined yet

friend_member_function_01.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Display; // only a forward declaration

class Storage {
  private:
    int int_value{};
    double double_value{};

  public:
    Storage(int i, double d) : int_value{i}, double_value{d} {}
    friend void Display::show(const Storage& s) const; // error!
};

class Display {
  public:
    void show(const Storage& s) const {
        std::cout << s.int_value << ' ' << s.double_value << '\n';
    }
};

int main() {
    Display{}.show(Storage{5, 6.7});
    return 0;
}
error: invalid use of incomplete type 'class Display'

To befriend Display::show, the compiler must have seen the full definition of Display, not just a forward declaration.

4.12 Attempt 2: swap the classes around

friend_member_function_02.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Display {
  public:
    void show(const Storage& s) const { // error: what is a Storage?
        std::cout << s.int_value << ' ' << s.double_value << '\n';
    }
};

class Storage {
  private:
    int int_value{};
    double double_value{};

  public:
    Storage(int i, double d) : int_value{i}, double_value{d} {}
    friend void Display::show(const Storage& s) const;
};

int main() {
    Display{}.show(Storage{5, 6.7});
    return 0;
}
error: 'Storage' does not name a type

Now Display::show() mentions Storage before the compiler has heard of it.

4.13 Attempt 3: declare first, define later

friend_member_function_03.cpp
#include <iostream>

class Storage; // 1. a forward declaration of Storage

class Display {
  public:
    void show(const Storage& s) const; // 2. declared, not defined yet
};

class Storage {
  private:
    int int_value{};
    double double_value{};

  public:
    Storage(int i, double d) : int_value{i}, double_value{d} {}
    friend void Display::show(const Storage& s) const; // fine now
};

void Display::show(const Storage& s) const { // 3. defined after Storage
    std::cout << s.int_value << ' ' << s.double_value << '\n';
}

int main() {
    Display{}.show(Storage{5, 6.7});
    return 0;
}
5 6.7
  1. Forward-declare Storage.
  2. Declare show().
  3. Define it after Storage.

5 Wrapping up

5.1 Summary

  • this points at the implicit object. Write it when a parameter hides a member, and return *this by reference to allow method chaining.
  • A destructor ~ClassName() runs automatically when an object is destroyed. Objects in a block are destroyed in reverse order.
  • RAII: acquire resources in the constructor and release them in the destructor. If you write a destructor, think about copying (rule of three); better, own nothing by hand (rule of zero).
  • A class template is a recipe for classes: Pair<int>, std::pair<int, double>, std::vector<double>.
  • A friend function or class may use a class’s private members. Friendship is granted, not taken. Prefer non-friends when public members are enough.

5.2 Keep learning

Explore these on your own, with Google Gemini in Guided Learning mode or on learncpp.com:

  1. The hidden this pointer and member function chaining
  2. Destructors, and the rule of three
  3. Class templates
  4. Friend classes and friend member functions
